meta.title: Subject-Verb Agreement Test
meta.description: A comprehensive 30-question test covering singular/plural subject-verb agreement, compound subjects (and, or, nor), indefinite pronouns, collective nouns, and subjects with intervening phrases.

details_explanation.explanation: The phrase 'the number of' takes a singular verb because 'number' is the head noun, not the plural noun that follows it.
details_explanation.introduction: Subject-verb agreement requires the verb to match the subject in number. Certain phrases like 'the number of' and 'a number of' follow different rules.

rules.title: 1. 'The number of' + plural noun
rules.explanation: When 'the number of' is followed by a plural noun, the subject is 'number' (singular), so the verb must be singular.
rules.structure: The number of + plural noun + singular verb
notes: 'The number of students is increasing' — 'is' agrees with 'number'.
Do not confuse with 'a number of' which takes a plural verb.

rules.title: 2. 'A number of' + plural noun
rules.explanation: When 'a number of' is followed by a plural noun, the subject is the plural noun, so the verb must be plural.
rules.structure: A number of + plural noun + plural verb
notes: 'A number of students are absent' — 'are' agrees with 'students'.

common_mistakes.wrong: The number of cars on the road are increasing.
common_mistakes.correct: The number of cars on the road is increasing.

other_examples.sentence: The number of applicants has increased significantly.
other_examples.translation: Jumlah pelamar telah meningkat secara signifikan.

other_examples.sentence: A number of issues remain unresolved.
other_examples.translation: Sejumlah masalah masih belum terselesaikan.

details_explanation.explanation: The indefinite pronoun 'each' is always singular, even when followed by a plural noun phrase. Therefore, it requires a singular verb.
details_explanation.introduction: Indefinite pronouns such as 'each', 'everyone', 'everybody', 'someone', 'nobody', etc., are grammatically singular and take singular verbs.

rules.title: 1. Indefinite pronouns ending in -one, -body, -thing
rules.explanation: Pronouns like 'everyone', 'someone', 'nobody', and 'everything' are singular and require singular verbs.
rules.structure: Everyone/Someone/Nobody + singular verb
notes: 'Everyone is here' — not 'Everyone are here'.
These pronouns do not take plural verbs even when referring to multiple people.

rules.title: 2. 'Each' and 'Every' as determiners
rules.explanation: When 'each' or 'every' modifies a singular noun, the subject is singular.
rules.structure: Each/Every + singular noun + singular verb
notes: 'Each student has a book' — 'has' is singular.
With 'each of + plural noun', the verb remains singular: 'Each of the boys is here'.

common_mistakes.wrong: Each of the students have a laptop.
common_mistakes.correct: Each of the students has a laptop.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Each' is singular, so the verb must be 'has'.

details_explanation.explanation: Collective nouns like 'committee', 'team', 'family', and 'government' are treated as singular when the group acts as a single unit. In this case, 'has' is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: Collective nouns refer to groups of people or things. In American English, they typically take singular verbs when acting as one unit.

rules.title: 1. Collective nouns as singular
rules.explanation: When a collective noun refers to the group as a single entity, use a singular verb.
rules.structure: Collective noun (acting as one) + singular verb
notes: 'The team is winning' — the team acts as one unit.
Common collective nouns: team, family, committee, government, audience, staff.

rules.title: 2. Collective nouns as plural
rules.explanation: When the members of the group act individually, the collective noun can take a plural verb (more common in British English).
rules.structure: Collective noun (acting individually) + plural verb
notes: 'The team are arguing among themselves' — members act individually.
In American English, singular verb is preferred unless emphasizing individual actions.

common_mistakes.wrong: The committee have made their decision.
common_mistakes.correct: The committee has made its decision.
common_mistakes.reason: The committee acts as one unit, so use singular verb and pronoun.

details_explanation.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. Here, 'employees' is plural and closer to the verb, so 'were' is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: When subjects are joined by 'or', 'nor', 'either...or', or 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearest subject (the principle of proximity).

rules.title: 1. Proximity rule for or/nor
rules.explanation: The verb agrees with the subject that is closest to it in the sentence.
rules.structure: Either S1 or S2 + verb (agrees with S2)
notes: 'Neither the students nor the teacher is here' — 'teacher' is closer, so 'is'.
'Neither the teacher nor the students are here' — 'students' is closer, so 'are'.

rules.title: 2. Compound subjects with 'and'
rules.explanation: Subjects joined by 'and' are plural and take a plural verb.
rules.structure: S1 and S2 + plural verb
notes: 'The cat and the dog are playing' — both subjects combine to form a plural subject.
Exception: If the two nouns refer to the same person/thing, use singular: 'The bread and butter is delicious'.

common_mistakes.wrong: Neither the players nor the coach were satisfied.
common_mistakes.correct: Neither the players nor the coach was satisfied.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Coach' is the nearer subject and is singular, so 'was'.

other_examples.translation: Baik makanan maupun minuman tidak disediakan.

details_explanation.explanation: The subject is 'bouquet' (singular), not 'roses'. Prepositional phrases like 'of roses' do not affect the number of the subject.
details_explanation.introduction: When a subject is followed by a prepositional phrase or other intervening phrase, the verb must still agree with the actual subject, not the object of the preposition.

rules.title: 1. Ignore intervening phrases
rules.explanation: Phrases between the subject and verb do not change the subject's number.
rules.structure: Subject + (prepositional phrase) + verb
notes: 'The box of chocolates is on the table' — 'box' is the subject.
'The students in the library are studying' — 'students' is the subject.

rules.title: 2. Common intervening phrases
rules.explanation: Phrases beginning with 'of', 'with', 'along with', 'together with', 'as well as', 'including', and 'in addition to' do not change the subject number.
rules.structure: Subject + as well as/together with/along with + noun + verb (agrees with subject)
notes: 'The teacher, along with the students, is going on a trip.' — subject is 'teacher' (singular).
'The CEO, as well as the managers, was present.' — subject is 'CEO' (singular).

common_mistakes.wrong: The list of items are on the desk.
common_mistakes.correct: The list of items is on the desk.
common_mistakes.reason: 'List' is singular; 'items' is part of the prepositional phrase and does not affect the verb.

details_explanation.explanation: The indefinite pronoun 'everyone' is always singular and takes a singular verb, even though it refers to many people.
details_explanation.introduction: Indefinite pronouns such as 'everyone', 'everybody', 'someone', 'somebody', 'anyone', 'anybody', 'no one', and 'nobody' are grammatically singular.

rules.title: 1. Everyone/Everybody + singular verb
rules.explanation: These pronouns are treated as singular subjects.
rules.structure: Everyone/Everybody + singular verb
notes: 'Everyone is invited' — not 'Everyone are invited'.
Even though 'everyone' means 'all people', the grammar is singular.

rules.title: 2. Pronoun agreement with indefinite pronouns
rules.explanation: Traditional grammar uses singular pronouns (his/her), but modern usage often accepts 'their' as a gender-neutral pronoun.
rules.structure: Everyone + singular verb + their/his or her
notes: 'Everyone has their own opinion' is widely accepted in modern English.
In formal writing, 'his or her' may be preferred.

multiErrorSegments.text: The teacher, along with the students,

details_explanation.explanation: The phrase 'along with the students' is an intervening phrase and does not change the number of the subject. The subject is 'teacher' (singular), so the verb must be 'is'.
details_explanation.introduction: Phrases like 'along with', 'together with', 'as well as', 'in addition to', and 'accompanied by' introduce additional information but do not make a singular subject plural.

rules.title: 1. 'Along with' / 'Together with' do not compound the subject
rules.explanation: These phrases are parenthetical and do not affect subject-verb agreement.
rules.structure: Singular subject + along with/together with + noun + singular verb
notes: 'The president, along with his advisors, is speaking.' — subject is 'president'.
'The cat, together with the kittens, is sleeping.' — subject is 'cat'.

rules.title: 2. Difference from 'and'
rules.explanation: 'And' joins two subjects into a compound subject (plural), while 'along with' does not.
rules.structure: S1 and S2 + plural verb vs. S1 along with S2 + singular verb
notes: 'The teacher and the student are here' (plural).
'The teacher along with the student is here' (singular).

common_mistakes.wrong: The CEO, as well as the directors, were present.
common_mistakes.correct: The CEO, as well as the directors, was present.
common_mistakes.reason: 'As well as' does not make the subject plural; the subject is 'CEO'.

details_explanation.introduction: Indefinite pronouns like 'some', 'all', 'most', 'none', 'any', and 'more' can be singular or plural depending on the noun they refer to.

rules.title: 1. 'Some of' + uncountable/singular noun

rules.title: 2. 'Some of' + plural noun
rules.explanation: When 'some of' refers to a plural noun, the verb is plural.
rules.structure: Some of + plural noun + plural verb
notes: 'Some of the students are absent.'
'Some of the books were damaged.'

details_explanation.explanation: Two subjects joined by 'and' form a compound subject, which is plural and requires a plural verb.
details_explanation.introduction: When two or more subjects are connected by 'and', they form a compound subject that takes a plural verb.

rules.title: 1. Compound subjects with 'and'
rules.explanation: Subjects joined by 'and' are treated as plural.
rules.structure: S1 and S2 + plural verb
notes: 'The dog and the cat are playing.'
'John and Mary are married.'

rules.title: 2. Exception: Same person or thing
rules.explanation: If the two nouns joined by 'and' refer to the same person or a single idea, the verb is singular.
rules.structure: S1 and S2 (same entity) + singular verb
notes: 'The bread and butter is delicious.' (one item)
'My friend and colleague is here.' (one person)

common_mistakes.wrong: The teacher and the student was talking.

details_explanation.explanation: The noun 'police' is always plural in English and requires a plural verb.
details_explanation.introduction: Some nouns are always plural and take plural verbs, even though they look singular. These include 'police', 'people', 'cattle', and 'clergy'.

rules.title: 1. Nouns always plural
rules.explanation: Certain nouns refer to groups of people or animals and are always treated as plural.
rules.structure: Plural-only noun + plural verb
notes: 'The police are coming.'
'People are waiting.'
'Cattle are grazing.'

rules.title: 2. Collective nouns that are always plural
rules.explanation: Unlike collective nouns like 'team' which can be singular or plural, these nouns are always plural.
rules.structure: Always-plural noun + plural verb
notes: 'The clergy are divided on the issue.'
Do not use 'police is' or 'people is'.

multiErrorSegments.text: The book, including all its illustrations,

details_explanation.explanation: The subject is 'book' (singular). The phrase 'including all its illustrations' is an intervening phrase and does not affect the verb.
details_explanation.introduction: Phrases beginning with 'including', 'such as', 'like', 'especially', and 'particularly' provide additional information but do not change the subject's number.

rules.title: 1. 'Including' introduces extra information
rules.explanation: The verb must agree with the main subject, not the items listed after 'including'.
rules.structure: Singular subject + including + noun(s) + singular verb
notes: 'The team, including its coach, is ready.'
'The house, including the gardens, is for sale.'

rules.title: 2. Identifying the true subject
rules.explanation: To find the subject, remove the intervening phrase and check the verb agreement.
rules.structure: Remove the phrase and verify: Subject + verb
notes: 'The book is quite expensive' — correct.
'The books, including the red one, are on the shelf.'

rules.title: 1. Everybody/Somebody/Nobody + singular verb

rules.structure: Everybody/Somebody/Nobody + singular verb
notes: 'Everybody is welcome.'

details_explanation.explanation: The collective noun 'government' is treated as singular in American English when acting as a single unit, so it takes 'has'.
details_explanation.introduction: Collective nouns like 'government', 'team', 'committee', and 'family' are singular when the group acts as one entity.

rules.title: 1. Collective nouns in American English
rules.explanation: In American English, collective nouns take singular verbs.
rules.structure: Collective noun + singular verb (American English)
notes: 'The government has decided.'
'The team is winning.'
'The family is eating dinner.'

rules.title: 2. Collective nouns in British English
rules.explanation: In British English, collective nouns can take plural verbs when members act individually.
rules.structure: Collective noun + plural verb (British English, individual action)
notes: 'The government are divided.' (British English)
'The team are playing well.' (British English)

multiErrorSegments.text: Either the cat or the dogs

details_explanation.explanation: With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Dogs' is plural and closer to the verb, so 'are' is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: When two subjects are joined by 'or', 'nor', 'either...or', or 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it.

rules.title: 1. Proximity rule
rules.explanation: The verb agrees with the nearest subject.
rules.structure: Either S1 or S2 + verb (agrees with S2)
notes: 'Either the students or the teacher is here.' — 'teacher' is closer.
'Either the teacher or the students are here.' — 'students' is closer.

rules.title: 2. Maintaining parallel structure
rules.explanation: For clarity, place the plural subject closer to the verb or rephrase the sentence.
rules.structure: Either + singular + or + plural + plural verb
notes: 'Either the manager or the employees are responsible.'
Avoid mixing singular and plural subjects when possible.

common_mistakes.wrong: Either the boys or the girl are coming.

common_mistakes.reason: 'Girl' is closer to the verb and is singular.

rules.title: 1. Nouns ending in -s that are singular
rules.explanation: Certain nouns ending in -s are treated as singular because they represent a single concept or field of study.

rules.explanation: Unlike 'scissors' or 'pants' which are plural, 'news' and academic subjects are singular.
rules.structure: Check meaning: single concept = singular verb
notes: 'Economics is a complex subject.'
'Politics is often controversial.'

details_explanation.introduction: When subjects are joined by 'and', they form a compound subject and take a plural verb, unless they refer to the same entity.

rules.title: 1. 'Both...and' emphasizes plurality
rules.explanation: The construction 'both...and' always creates a plural subject.
rules.structure: Both S1 and S2 + plural verb
notes: 'Both the students and the teacher are here.'
'Both the cat and the dog are sleeping.'

rules.title: 2. Compound subjects with 'and'
rules.explanation: Two distinct subjects joined by 'and' require a plural verb.
rules.structure: S1 and S2 + plural verb
notes: 'The manager and the assistant are working.'
'The sun and the moon are visible.'

common_mistakes.wrong: Both the mother and the father was present.
common_mistakes.correct: Both the mother and the father were present.
common_mistakes.reason: Two subjects joined by 'and' require a plural verb.

multiErrorSegments.text: Neither the president nor the ministers

details_explanation.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'Ministers' is plural and closer to the verb, so 'have' is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: In 'neither...nor' constructions, the verb agrees with the subject closest to it.

rules.title: 1. Proximity rule with 'neither...nor'
rules.explanation: The verb matches the number of the nearest subject.
rules.structure: Neither S1 nor S2 + verb (agrees with S2)
notes: 'Neither the teacher nor the students are here.' — 'students' is closer.
'Neither the students nor the teacher is here.' — 'teacher' is closer.

rules.title: 2. Practice tip
rules.explanation: Mentally remove the first subject to check the verb agreement with the second.
rules.structure: Remove S1: Nor S2 + verb
notes: 'Nor the ministers have responded' — correct.
'Nor the minister has responded' — correct.

common_mistakes.correct: Neither the cat nor the dogs are outside.

details_explanation.explanation: The noun 'scissors' is always plural and takes a plural verb.
details_explanation.introduction: Some nouns are always plural because they refer to objects with two parts. These include 'scissors', 'pants', 'trousers', 'glasses' (eyewear), and 'pliers'.

rules.title: 1. Always-plural nouns (two-part objects)
rules.explanation: These nouns are grammatically plural and require plural verbs.
rules.structure: Plural-only noun + plural verb
notes: 'The scissors are sharp.'
'My glasses are broken.'
'The pants are too long.'

rules.title: 2. 'A pair of' changes the number
rules.explanation: When preceded by 'a pair of', the subject becomes singular.
rules.structure: A pair of + plural noun + singular verb
notes: 'A pair of scissors is on the table.'
'A pair of pants was bought.'

common_mistakes.correct: The scissors are in the drawer.

details_explanation.explanation: The subject is 'quality' (singular). The phrase 'of the products' is a prepositional phrase and does not affect the verb.
details_explanation.introduction: When the subject is followed by a prepositional phrase, the verb agrees with the subject, not the object of the preposition.

rules.title: 1. Identify the true subject
rules.explanation: The subject is the noun before the prepositional phrase.
rules.structure: Subject + of + noun + verb (agrees with subject)
notes: 'The quality of the products has improved.' — subject is 'quality'.
'The color of the flowers is beautiful.' — subject is 'color'.

rules.title: 2. Common prepositional phrases
rules.explanation: Phrases beginning with 'of', 'in', 'on', 'at', 'from', 'with', etc., do not affect subject-verb agreement.
rules.structure: Subject + prepositional phrase + verb
notes: 'The box of chocolates is on the table.'
'The students in the classroom are quiet.'

details_explanation.explanation: The pronoun 'all' can be singular or plural depending on the noun it refers to. 'Information' is uncountable/singular, so the verb is 'was'.
details_explanation.introduction: Indefinite pronouns like 'all', 'some', 'most', 'none', 'any', and 'more' can be singular or plural depending on the noun they refer to.

rules.title: 1. 'All of' + uncountable/singular noun
rules.explanation: When 'all of' refers to an uncountable noun, use a singular verb.
rules.structure: All of + uncountable noun + singular verb
notes: 'All of the water is gone.'
'All of the information was accurate.'

rules.title: 2. 'All of' + plural noun
rules.explanation: When 'all of' refers to a plural noun, use a plural verb.
rules.structure: All of + plural noun + plural verb
notes: 'All of the students are present.'
'All of the books were sold.'

common_mistakes.correct: All of the furniture was expensive.

details_explanation.explanation: The collective noun 'family' is treated as singular when acting as a single unit. The word 'together' reinforces this unity.
details_explanation.introduction: Collective nouns like 'family', 'team', 'committee', and 'audience' are singular when the group acts as one.

rules.title: 1. Collective nouns as single units
rules.explanation: When the group acts as one, use a singular verb.
rules.structure: Collective noun (acting as one) + singular verb
notes: 'The family is eating dinner.'
'The team is winning.'
'The committee has decided.'

rules.title: 2. Words indicating unity
rules.explanation: Words like 'together', 'as one', and 'united' indicate the group acts as a unit, requiring a singular verb.
rules.structure: Collective noun + together/as one + singular verb
notes: 'The family is going together.'
'The team is united in its decision.'

common_mistakes.reason: In American English, 'family' as a single unit takes a singular verb.

details_explanation.introduction: Indefinite pronouns 'either' and 'neither' are singular and require singular verbs.

rules.title: 2. 'Neither of' + plural noun

details_explanation.explanation: Two subjects joined by 'and' form a compound subject and take a plural verb.
details_explanation.introduction: When two distinct subjects are connected by 'and', the verb must be plural.

rules.title: 1. Compound subjects with 'and'
rules.explanation: Two separate entities joined by 'and' are plural.
rules.structure: S1 and S2 + plural verb
notes: 'Tom and Jerry are friends.'
'The cat and the dog are playing.'

rules.title: 2. Identifying compound subjects
rules.explanation: Look for the conjunction 'and' connecting two subjects.
rules.structure: Subject 1 + and + Subject 2 + plural verb
notes: 'The teacher and the student are talking.'
'The sun and the moon are bright.'

details_explanation.explanation: The subject is 'the number' (singular), not 'people'. The phrase 'of people attending the event' modifies 'number' but does not change its grammatical number.
details_explanation.introduction: 'The number of' is always followed by a singular verb, while 'a number of' is followed by a plural verb.

rules.title: 1. 'The number of' + plural noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: 'The number' is the subject and is singular.

rules.title: 2. 'A number of' + plural noun + plural verb

details_explanation.explanation: The indefinite pronoun 'anyone' is singular and takes a singular verb.
details_explanation.introduction: Indefinite pronouns ending in '-one' (anyone, everyone, someone, no one) are grammatically singular.

rules.title: 1. Anyone/Everyone/Someone + singular verb
rules.explanation: These pronouns are treated as singular subjects.
rules.structure: Anyone/Everyone/Someone + singular verb
notes: 'Anyone is welcome to join.'

rules.title: 2. Compound structures with indefinite pronouns
rules.explanation: Even with a relative clause, the main verb agrees with the singular pronoun.
rules.structure: Anyone who + verb (in relative clause) + singular verb (main clause)
notes: 'Anyone who wants to come is invited.'
'Everyone who has finished may leave.'

details_explanation.explanation: No error. In British English, collective nouns like 'staff' can take a plural verb when members act individually. In American English, 'staff' is typically singular: 'The staff is attending.' Both forms can be acceptable depending on context and regional convention.
details_explanation.introduction: Collective nouns can take singular or plural verbs depending on whether the group is viewed as a unit or as individuals.

rules.title: 1. American English: Collective nouns as singular
rules.explanation: In American English, collective nouns take singular verbs.
rules.structure: Collective noun + singular verb (American English)
notes: 'The staff is attending the meeting.'
'The team is practicing.'

rules.title: 2. British English: Collective nouns as plural
rules.explanation: In British English, collective nouns often take plural verbs, especially when emphasizing individual members.
rules.structure: Collective noun + plural verb (British English)
notes: 'The staff are attending the meeting.'
'The team are practicing.'

common_mistakes.wrong: The staff is attending (in British English context where plural is expected).
common_mistakes.correct: The staff are attending (British English) or The staff is attending (American English).
common_mistakes.reason: Regional differences affect collective noun agreement.
